name: Victor Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate Chinese into English for small game studios and app makers, mostly menus, item descriptions and in-game dialogue. My day starts with a big batch of strings through an AI model I've set up with the studio's glossary, then I go line by line fixing tone and jokes. In the afternoon I sometimes do video-call interpreting for a studio talking to its Shanghai publisher. Sam, my boyfriend, fixes bikes at a shop on the corner, so he's out the door at eight and I'm at the desk by the window.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love when a fantasy character gets a voice in English that players quote on forums. I'm fast with the tools, which covers for the fact that my Chinese still isn't as deep as the senior people's, especially classical references. What wears me out is studios wanting a whole patch overnight because the AI made them think it's instant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was a good assistant that got oversold, and that the people who used it well are fine. I'd post my workflow on the localisation forum, because people always ask. I'd probably be a bit smug about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that version is good for me. I'm one of the people who already uses the tools every day, so I'd be faster than juniors who don't. My income would stay where it is or go up a bit, because studios would still need someone to make the dialogue sound human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my studio clients and pitch two more, using my speed as the selling point. I'd put about two hundred a month into an index fund, since my savings are only about four months. I'd also spend evenings on classical Chinese, because that's where I'm weak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Maybe a bit bored, because I like it when things move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the overnight patches wear you out. Does that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, if anything it gets worse, because the tools make clients think everything is instant. Last month a studio sent four thousand strings at six in the evening and wanted them by morning. I did it, but Sam found me asleep on the sofa with the laptop on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Sam make of your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam thinks it's funny that I argue with a computer all day about whether a sword sounds noble enough. Sam's job is all hands, so we joke that he'll still be fixing bikes when I'm replaced. It's a joke, mostly.

I'd share my **workflow** on the localisation forum, a bit smugly.
think: Being a **daily AI user**, I'd be faster than juniors who don't.
My **income** would hold or rise, since studios still need human dialogue.
do: Pitch **two more studios** using speed as the selling point.
Invest about **two hundred a month** in an index fund.
Study **classical Chinese** in the evenings to fill a weak spot.
feel: **Calm**, maybe a bit bored, since he likes change.

fieldNote: One of the few in his line who feels **secure** in the mild picture, because of his tool skill.

Knows his **weak spot** is classical references and plans to fix it.

steps.text: Pitch two more game studios on fast turnaround
Put about two hundred a month into an index fund
Study classical Chinese in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say translators need to learn the tools or get left behind, but also that studios shouldn't use AI to pay us pennies. I'd say both online, which annoys both sides. I'd also say we need a union that covers freelancers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in the danger zone. Being fast with AI is my edge, but in that picture every studio has the same AI. And my Chinese isn't strong enough to be the expert they keep for the hard parts. I could see my rate halving inside two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move up the chain fast: offer studios full localisation management, setting up their AI pipeline and checking quality across languages. I'd do a short course in game production, around five hundred, and join the freelancers' union. I'd keep investing, but smaller, and build savings to six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way that makes me want to move rather than hide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the expert they keep for the hard parts. Who is that, in your world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone like Wei, who I worked with on a fantasy game last year. Wei grew up reading the classics and can catch a reference to a Tang poem in a sword's name. I can't do that yet, and the AI can't either, but in this picture the AI gets closer every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the rate halves, what changes at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam and I would stop talking about getting a bigger flat with a second room. I'd stop the takeaway habit, which is honestly most weeknights. We'd still be okay because Sam's wage is steady, but I'd hate being the one who brings in less.

say: I'd say translators must **learn the tools**, and studios mustn't pay pennies.
I'd call for a **freelancers' union** that covers people like me.
think: My **AI edge** vanishes when every studio has the same tool.
I could see my **rate halving** inside two years.
do: Offer studios **localisation management**, running their AI pipeline and quality checks.
Take a **game production course** for about five hundred.
Build savings to **six months** and invest smaller amounts.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a way that pushes him to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a basic income, full stop. I'd be loud about it, and I'd say tech companies should pay into it. At the studios I'd say less, because there probably wouldn't be many studio calls left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my job ends the day it arrives. Everything I do is screen work, and AGI by 2028 means the studios can run the AI themselves without a pipeline person. The three years before robots are useless to me unless I learn a trade now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the next two years earning as much as I can while the work lasts, and pushing savings to nine months. I'd look at something hands-on, maybe working with Sam at the bike shop, since Sam's boss is always short-handed. Once it arrives, I'd sign up for any support and join the campaign for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm the guy who loves new tech, and AGI would eat me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go and fix bikes. How serious is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More serious than it sounds. I already true my own wheels, and the shop needs someone to do the online orders and the repairs. It wouldn't pay like translation, but it would buy me those three years until the robots, and maybe longer if people want a person who knows their bike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction in loving the tools and fearing this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, totally. I'd still use it every day and still be amazed. You can be amazed by a wave and still not want to be under it.

I'd say **less at the studios**, as few calls would be left.
think: My job **ends on arrival**, since it's all screen work.

Sign up for **support** and join the basic income campaign.
feel: **Alarmed**, as a tech lover about to be eaten by the tech.
S2.quote: I'm the guy who loves new tech, and AGI would eat me.
fieldNote: He names the **contradiction** himself: amazed by the tool and afraid of it.
His fallback, **bike repairs**, uses the robot delay deliberately.
Wants a **basic income** funded by tech firms, in line with his views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up something smart, and I'd tell younger translators to start planning now. I'd still argue for a basic income, but less angrily. I'd write a long post on how I'd use the five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a real window. I could earn well from the studios for three years, because the tools would be messy and they'd need a fixer. Then I'd need to be somewhere AI can't easily reach, ideally with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every studio contract going for three years and save hard. I'd do a cycle mechanic certificate in the evenings in year two, which costs about six hundred, and talk to Sam's boss about buying into the shop. I'd keep putting money into the index fund too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind I can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying into the shop. Where does that money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the three good years, mostly. If I put away about a thousand a month at studio rates, by 2030 I'd have enough to buy a share. It's a risk, but I like risks, and it's one Sam would be part of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the junior translators you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to wait for the job to end. The best time to move is while you still have something to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd want governments funding retraining and a basic income trial now. Online I'd be an optimist again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I could have a whole career in localisation management before it ends. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI arrives, with savings and probably a share in something. It still ends my line of work, but not my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd climb into localisation management over the next four years, running teams and AI pipelines for a mid-size studio. I'd invest steadily and maybe buy a flat with Sam. Around 2032 I'd start learning a trade properly, so I'm ready before the robots in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, honestly. In ten years the ending is the same, but I'd get to write it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said buy a flat with Sam. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a real wish. Sam and I have looked at two-bedroom places near the park. In this picture I'd feel able to take on a mortgage, which I wouldn't in the fast ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk you're not seeing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that everyone has the same idea and the management jobs vanish first. Managers are thinking workers too. I'd keep the trade plan as backup, so I'm not betting on one thing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have nothing to sell and no time to build anything. What would help is a basic income or at least a long, paid retraining scheme. I'd also want the AI companies to pay for it, since they'd be the ones making the money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how odd it is to train the thing that replaces you. Every correction I make to the AI's game dialogue probably goes back into making it better, and I've never been paid for that part.
